rationale: Round 0 compiled and ran correctly with no ICE fallback, so the safe move is to push obfuscation intensity up while protecting the hot core of mst (Do_all_BlueRule, HashLookup, HashInsert run in the innermost loops of the benchmark). SUB gets the highest security/diversity weights since instruction substitution is cheap in both time and space and carries near-zero correctness risk on this tiny 428-line, 11-function program, making it the workhorse pass applied broadly. IBR and IGV are raised next: opaque branching and global-variable indirection add strong static-analysis resistance at low runtime/size cost, and IGV notably hardens the graph/node data structures central to mst without touching per-iteration latency much. FLA and BCF get high security weights but elevated RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights (0.6-0.65) so the selector still applies them where they pay off (the large MakeGraph, MakeHash, Do_all_BlueRule bodies) yet throttles them on tight hot loops where flattening dispatch and bogus predicate evaluation would hurt benchmark latency. SPLIT stays a cheap diversity amplifier with modest security weight, applied broadly to break up basic-block contiguity that SUB alone leaves behind. ICALL keeps moderate security weight but the highest CorrectnessRisk (0.3) and elevated RuntimeCost (0.55): indirect-call transformation on a program with hash-table function pointers and recursive BlueRule calls risks both miscompilation and call-overhead, so it is favored mainly on cold setup functions (args.c, MakeGraph setup) rather than the lookup/insert hot path. Overall this shifts the mix from round 0's baseline toward more control-flow and data-level obfuscation while cost weights keep the aggressive passes out of the innermost loops, preserving acceptable runtime and size on a 2 KB text section that has headroom for moderate growth.
